chapter_theme: Ainkurunuru 161 to 170, the neythal decade of the small white gull: each poem opens on the gull of the great sea's shore at rest, feeding, sleeping, nesting or taking fright, and by our reading the woman (twice her friend) weighs the shore lord's word against her wasting body: bangles that leave as he left, words that have changed, gossip bred by his good name, pallid eyes that do not obey her trust.

161.reading: The woman says that for the lord of the ford where the small white gull of the great sea's shore rests on the black-branched punnai, her forehead, once spread with pallor, has wasted away, and the heart that desired him has gone over to sickness.
161.nuance: The gull has a fixed perch on the punnai while her heart has none; the decade's refrain sets every poem against this bird that always has somewhere to rest. Read as scene: the gull only rests, it does nothing a person of the situation does.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore gull resting on the punnai

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the first person (the heart that desired him, நயந்த நெஞ்சம், is her own) marks the woman herself as speaker, and her friend as the one she talks to

162.reading: The woman says that the words of the lord of the ford, where the small white gull picks its food from the flowing dark backwater and then sleeps in the fragrant grove, have become something else.
162.nuance: Near miss for ullurai: the gull that feeds in one place and sleeps in another fragrant one can be read as the man who takes his pleasure elsewhere, but only one correspondence can be named, so condition 3 fails and the bird stays scene.

thinai_evidence.note: the gull feeding in the backwater

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; a woman judging the lover's changed word, as the heroine does throughout the decade

163.reading: The woman says that because the lord of the ford, where the small white gull sleeps through the roar of the backwater's spray, has abandoned her, the bangles too have abandoned her shapely forearm.
163.nuance: The verb துற is used twice, துறந்தென துறந்து: the bangles copy his act, so her wasting body becomes a second desertion, and the pun on துறைவன் (lord of the ford) makes his title name the deed.

thinai_evidence.note: the gull asleep by the spray of the backwater

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the first person (என் முன்கை, my forearm) marks the woman herself as speaker, and her friend as the one she talks to

iraicchi.act: the gull sleeps undisturbed through the roar of the spray
iraicchi.sense: the man who left sleeps as easily, untouched by the uproar his leaving has raised in her

164.reading: The speaker says that the fitness of the cool lord of the ford, where the small white gull feeds on ayirai fish at the edge of the dark backwater, did not stay a matter between them but has bred gossip.
164.nuance: தகுதி, his fitness or worth, is the thing that has gone public: the praise of the man is itself what the town now talks about, so the gossip is born of his good name, not his fault.

thinai_evidence.note: the gull feeding on backwater fish

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; நம்மோடு (with us) is the woman's or her friend's word for their side, and alar places the poem in secret love; read as the woman to her friend

165.reading: The woman says that the word spoken by the lord of the ford, where the small white gull gorges on the little fish of the drying backwater, has taken the bright bangles from her wrist.
165.nuance: She blames the word, not the man: a promise unkept is the thief of the bangles, so the poem makes speech the agent of her wasting. The gull eating its fill of small fish from a drying pool is left as scene.

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the first person (என் இறையோர் எல்வளை, my bangles) marks the woman herself as speaker, and her friend as the one she talks to

166.reading: Having come to trust the gentle lord of the shore, where the small white gull takes fright at the striped white thaali, thinking it a net, the good woman's eyes have become well again.
166.nuance: What the gull fears is uncertain: வரிவெண் தாலி may be a striped white shell or a plant of the shore; either way the point is that it is harmless and only looks like a net.

thinai_evidence.note: the shore gull afraid of a fisher's net

karu.sense: striped white thing, a shell or plant

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; நல்லோள் (the good woman) in the third person points to the friend, speaking of the heroine to someone outside the pair, perhaps the man or the household

iraicchi.act: the gull takes fright at a harmless white thing, mistaking it for a net
iraicchi.sense: her earlier fear of the man was a fear of a snare that was never there, and his word has now shown it harmless

167.reading: The woman says that the lord of the ford, where the small white gull feeds on shoals of ketiru fish in the dark backwater, spoke as if he would show grace and did not, yet he is still an old companion.
167.nuance: The final word turns the complaint: the broken promise is stated plainly, and then excused by the length of the bond, so the old tie survives the very failure she has just named.

thinai_evidence.note: the gull feeding on shoals of backwater fish

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the closing தொல் கேள் (old companion) defends the man, the heroine's answer to a friend who blames him

168.reading: If the cool lord of the ford, where the small white gull lays its eggs inside a boat moored at the landing, would show grace, the bright-browed girl would drink her milk again.
168.nuance: Refusing milk is the sign of a girl wasting in secret love; the friend names the cure as the man's grace, which in kalavu means marriage.

thinai_evidence.note: the gull nesting in a moored boat

thurai_akam.speaker: thozhi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; அரிவை (the girl) in the third person and the conditional நல்கின் (if he shows grace) point to the friend pressing the man on her behalf

iraicchi.act: the gull lays its eggs and makes its home in a boat at the ford
iraicchi.sense: even the gull settles its household at his landing, so he too should take her home and make a household with her

169.reading: The woman asks her friend why, though she knows the truth in the heart of the lord of the ford, where the small white gull, tired of the golden-clustered nyazhal, rests on the flowering punnai bough with its bursting buds, her eyes still turn pale.
169.nuance: Near miss for iraicchi: the gull that tires of one tree (முனையில்) and moves to another could carry a doubt of his constancy against her stated trust, but the act is not clearly one the man does or should do in the poem, so it stays scene. The poem's point is that knowledge does not govern the body.

thinai_evidence.note: the nyazhal and punnai trees of the shore

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; the poem names its addressee, தோழி, and the eyes are the speaker's own, என் கண்

170.reading: If you say he is good, the woman asks her friend, then why do her many-petalled, kohl-lined eyes turn pale over the lord of the ford, where the small white gull tears the neythal flowers of the dark backwater?
170.nuance: பல்லிதழ் (many-petalled) is the word for a flower, so her eyes are the neythal the gull tears; the friend's நல்லன் is answered by the image, not by argument.

thinai_evidence.note: the neythal flower of the backwater

comparisons.tenor: the man spoiling the woman whose eyes are neythal flowers

thurai_akam.speaker: thalaivi
thurai_akam.note: speaker inferred: the colophon gives no thurai; என்றி (you say) answers a friend who praises the man, and the eyes are the speaker's own

ullurai.tenor: the man the friend calls good, and the woman whose eyes he spoils

pairs.situation: the small white, harmless-seeming bird is the man the friend calls good
the neythal it tears is her flower-like eyes, now pallid

ullurai.speaker_fit: the heroine uses the gull and the neythal of her own shore, things she knows (porul 7.26)

links.note: Same situation and speaker: the woman of the shore says the lord of the ford (துறைவன்) has left her and her bangles slip from her forearm; the Kural keeps the Ainkurunuru's words துறைவன், துற, முன்கை, இறை and வளை.
links.teaches: The couplet lifts a neythal formula whole, but gives the bangles a new office: in the Ainkurunuru they imitate his desertion, in the Kural they broadcast it like gossip, so the later poet turned the body from mirror of the man into witness to the town.

links.note: The Kural tells friends to read a painful act of an old friend as folly or deep intimacy; the heroine of 167 calls the man who promised grace and gave none an old companion, தொல் கேள்.
links.teaches: The heroine applies the ethics book's rule of old friendship inside love, and the poem shows its cost: the same rule that keeps a long bond alive lets a broken promise go unanswered, so the wronged side carries the whole duty of forbearance.

links.note: In Akananuru 48 the foster mother asks why her daughter will not drink milk (பாலும் உண்ணாள்) and has paled; in 168 the friend tells the man that the girl will drink milk again if he shows grace.
links.teaches: Refusing milk is a fixed sign of secret love that the friend can turn two ways: toward the household, as the symptom she explains in disclosing the affair, and toward the lover, as the cure only he can give, so one sign drives both halves of the push toward marriage.

links.note: On the plain reading the claims are incompatible: in 170 the woman holds up her pallid eyes as evidence against the friend's word that he is good, while in Kural 1190 she would rather be called pallid than have the friend blame his unkindness.
links.teaches: Read together, the two show the heroine taking the side opposite to whoever speaks to her, so her pallor is not a fixed verdict on the man but an argument she turns against his praise or for his defence as the friend's stance requires.

links.note: In both the woman has accepted the man's part with her mind, in Kural 1181 by consenting to his absence, in 169 by knowing the truth of his heart, and still the pallor spreads on her.
links.teaches: The couplet makes her consent the reason she cannot complain of her pallor, and the Ainkurunuru adds that even trust in his heart does not stop it, so pallor in this tradition is a bodily fact beyond the will rather than a charge against the man.

source_issues: The colophon of every poem in this decade gives thinai only, no thurai; speaker and addressee are inferred from the poem and recorded in thurai_akam with a note.
165 line 4 reads இறையோர் where 163 line 4 has இறையேர் (fair-wristed) in the same phrase; likely a misprint for இறையேர்.
165 line 2 divides அறு கழிச் (the drying backwater) as two words; read as அறுகழி.
166 line 2 வரிவெண் தாலி: what the gull mistakes for a net is unclear (a striped white shell or a shore plant); the reading of the poem does not depend on it but the iraicchi's image does.
168 line 4 is divided பாலா ரும்மே; read as பால் ஆரும் (will drink milk).
